analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing workers and customers into arbitration to settle disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 38 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Judiciary Committee in February 2019 and never received a vote or a hearing before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would void contracts that force people to arbitrate disputes before they arise — the fine-print clauses most employers and many consumer companies require workers and customers to sign. It covers employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, and it also voids fine-print bans on joining class actions. After a dispute has actually happened, companies and individuals could still agree to arbitrate voluntarily.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers — including independent contractors — who could take wage theft, discrimination, and harassment claims to court instead of a private arbitrator; consumers and small businesses who could sue over credit, products, and services; and people harmed by price-fixing or discrimination who could again join class or collective actions instead of being pushed into one-at-a-time arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: No company could enforce a fine-print clause requiring arbitration of an employment dispute before it arises, so workers — including independent contractors — could bring wage, discrimination, and harassment claims in court.
Consumers could sue over credit, products, services, and investments, and could join class actions instead of being confined to individual arbitration.

Fine-print waivers that block participation in a joint, class, or collective action would be unenforceable, restoring class and collective lawsuits for antitrust, civil rights, wage, and consumer claims.

A court, not a company-chosen arbitrator, would decide whether these rules apply, closing the common practice of routing every challenge — including challenges to the arbitration clause itself — to the arbitrator.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers and consumer-facing companies — including gig-economy platforms, financial firms, and credit providers — would lose the ability to funnel disputes into private arbitration and block class actions, and would face more courtroom litigation and class action exposure. Professional arbitration providers would lose a large share of their business.

drawbacks.text: Court litigation is typically slower and more expensive than arbitration for an individual claim, and the bill would push more single-plaintiff disputes into that system; companies would also face far more class action exposure, a cost that can show up in prices and settlements.

The bill is broad: it covers independent contractors as well as employees and reaches nearly any consumer transaction, so even companies with well-regarded arbitration programs would lose the option entirely — though it preserves arbitration provisions in union collective bargaining agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded the speed and low cost arbitration can offer in individual cases for the public accountability of open court, including the leverage of class actions. For claims that are small dollar-by-dollar — most consumer and wage disputes — individual arbitration is often not economically rational, which is why supporters considered the trade worth making; the honest cost is more litigation expense and slower resolution in some cases.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on February 28, 2019, with 32 original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; that was the last action of any kind in its two-year history.
It attracted 38 cosponsors — 37 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republican signed on, and the committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that impose arbitration clauses kept the status quo: they can still require workers and customers to arbitrate individually and waive class actions, a system the bill would have ended.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 32 original cosponsors.

for.name: 38 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no further action was available to them.

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: Committee never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 supporters were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the committee chairmanship, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: Forced arbitration clauses let employers resolve wage, discrimination, and harassment claims privately and individually, which is far cheaper than defending class actions. The bill would have stripped that tool from every employment relationship, including contractors.

industries.industry: Financial services and consumer credit companies
industries.note: Bank, credit card, and brokerage agreements routinely require arbitration and class action waivers for consumer and securities disputes. The bill would have made those clauses unenforceable, reopening courtroom and class action claims.

Firms that administer forced arbitrations, and the arbitrators and defense-side practices built around them, would lose the high volume of mandatory cases the bill covers. Voluntary post-dispute arbitration would remain.
Restoring class and collective actions would create work for lawyers who bring them; that gain rides on the same court access the bill gives workers and consumers.
